<problem>
For each positive integer \(m\), let \(B_m\) be the finite simple graph with vertex set \(\{u,v,w_1,\ldots,w_m\}\) and edge set \(\{uv\}\cup\{uw_i,vw_i:1\le i\le m\}\). For finite simple graphs \(G,H\), define \(r(G,H)\) to be the least positive integer \(N\) such that every red-blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph \(K_N\) contains a red subgraph isomorphic to \(G\) or a blue subgraph isomorphic to \(H\); these copies need not be induced.

Determine explicitly, for every fixed real parameter \(0<\alpha\le1\), the asymptotic coefficient
\[
c(\alpha):=\lim_{\substack{n\to\infty\\ n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}}}\frac{r(B_{\lceil\alpha n\rceil},B_n)}{n}.
\]
Give a formula valid on the entire interval \((0,1]\), including all transition points exactly and specifying their endpoint cases.
</problem>

A complete answer to this problem: A complete answer must establish that the defining limit exists for every real α in (0,1] and give an explicit formula for c(α) throughout that interval. If the formula is piecewise, it must identify every transition point exactly and specify the value or applicable case at each endpoint.

3	Put
4	\[
5	\alpha_*=\frac{52-16\sqrt3}{121}=0.2007205543710575\ldots .

9	\boxed{

12	2,&0<\alpha\le \dfrac16,\\[2mm]
13	\dfrac{\bigl(\sqrt{3-2\alpha}+2\sqrt\alpha\bigr)^2}{3},
14	   &\dfrac16<\alpha<\alpha_*,\\[3mm]

18	The adjacent formulas agree at both transition points. In particular, the middle formula is also valid at either endpoint.
19	
20	The principal difficulty is the upper bound in the intermediate interval. We prove the requisite inequality below, rather than assume a sharp book-Ramsey theorem.
21	
22	## 1. A kernel formulation
23	
24	We use the standard compactness theorem for graphons: a sequence of finite graphs has a cut-convergent subsequence, and the density of each fixed graph is continuous under this convergence.
25	
26	For a symmetric measurable \(W:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]\), write
27	\[
28	C_R(x,y)=\int_0^1W(x,z)W(y,z)\,dz,
29	\quad
30	C_B(x,y)=\int_0^1(1-W(x,z))(1-W(y,z))\,dz.
31	\]
32	We say that \(W\) has book bounds \(a,b\) if, almost everywhere,
33	\[
34	W(x,y)>0\implies C_R(x,y)\le a,\qquad
35	W(x,y)<1\implies C_B(x,y)\le b.                 \tag{1}
36	\]
37	
38	Here is why this formulation applies. Suppose colorings on \(N_j\) vertices have no red \(B_{m_j}\) or blue \(B_{n_j}\), where
39	\[
40	\frac{m_j}{N_j}\longrightarrow a,\qquad
41	\frac{n_j}{N_j}\longrightarrow b.
42	\]
43	For every fixed positive integer \(k\), their red adjacency kernels satisfy
44	\[
45	t(B_k,W_j)
46	=\int W_j(x,y)C_{R,j}(x,y)^k\,dx\,dy
47	\le \left(\frac{m_j-1}{N_j}\right)^k\int W_j.
48	\]
49	Pass to a graphon limit, then let \(k\to\infty\). This gives the red implication in (1); the blue implication follows identically. The discrepancy on the diagonal squares of the finite kernels has measure \(1/N_j\), so the blue limit is \(1-W\).
50	
51	We shall prove the following sharp inequality.
52	
53	### Kernel lemma
54	Suppose \(W\) satisfies (1), and
55	\[
56	0<a\le b<\frac12,\qquad \sqrt a+\sqrt b<1.
57	\]
58	Set
59	\[
60	u_*=\frac4{\sqrt3}-2,\qquad A=u_*^2.
61	\]
62	Then necessarily
63	\[
64	a<A,\qquad
65	b\ge f(a):=1+2a-4\sqrt{\frac a3}.              \tag{2}
66	\]
67	
68	## 2. Preliminary structure
69	
70	For a vertex \(x\), let
71	\[
72	q_R(x)=\int W(x,z)^2\,dz,\qquad
73	q_B(x)=\int(1-W(x,z))^2\,dz.
74	\]
75	
76	### 2.1. The two vertex types
77	
78	Almost every vertex satisfies
79	\[
80	q_R(x)\le a\quad\hbox{or}\quad q_B(x)\le b.    \tag{3}
81	\]
82	Indeed, otherwise some positive-measure set has both inequalities violated by a fixed margin. The space of \(L^2\) row functions is separable, so a positive-measure subset has all its rows arbitrarily close in \(L^2\). Every pair in that subset then has both common-neighborhood integrals exceeding the corresponding bounds, contradicting (1).
83	
84	The alternatives in (3) are disjoint: Minkowski’s inequality gives
85	\[
86	1=\|W(x,\cdot)+(1-W(x,\cdot))\|_2
87	 \le\sqrt{q_R(x)}+\sqrt{q_B(x)}.
88	\]
89	
90	Let \(R\) be the first type and \(B\) the second, and put \(s=|R|\). The set \(R\) is a red clique almost everywhere. To see this, take red rows \(p,q\) of two vertices in \(R\), and put
91	\[
92	h=\frac{p+q}{2},\quad k=\frac{p-q}{2},\quad
93	v=\int h,\quad t=\sqrt a<\frac12.
94	\]
95	Then \(v\le t\) and \(\|h\|_2^2+\|k\|_2^2\le t^2\), so
96	\[
97	\begin{aligned}
98	\langle1-p,1-q\rangle
99	&=1-2v+\|h\|_2^2-\|k\|_2^2\\
100	&\ge1-2v+2v^2-t^2
101	 \ge(1-t)^2>b.
102	\end{aligned}
103	\]
104	Thus their connecting edge must be red. Consequently
105	\[
106	s\le a,\qquad
107	\int_B\int_R W(v,r)^2\,dr\,dv\le s(a-s).      \tag{4}
108	\]
109	
110	### 2.2. A clique inequality
111	
112	If \(k\) vertices in \(B\) form a red-support clique, then
113	\[
114	b+ra\ge\frac r{1+r}\qquad(0\le r\le k-1).    \tag{5}
115	\]
116	For completeness, put \(\lambda=2r/(k-1)\in[0,2]\). For arbitrary real \(z_i\),
117	\[
118	\sum_i(1-z_i)^2+\lambda\sum_{i<j}z_i z_j
119	\ge \frac{kr}{1+r}.
120	\]
121	This follows by first replacing \(\sum z_i^2\) by \((\sum z_i)^2/k\), then completing a square. Apply it to the \(k\) red rows and integrate.
122	
123	The red support on \(B\) is \(K_4\)-free. Otherwise (5) with \(k=4,r=3\) implies \(a>1/12\). We may then choose
124	\[
125	r=\frac1{\sqrt a}-1<3
126	\]
127	in (5), obtaining \(b\ge(1-\sqrt a)^2\), contrary to the hypothesis.
128	
129	## 3. Selecting three useful rows
130	
131	Put
132	\[
133	h(v)=\int_R W(v,r)^2\,dr.
134	\]
135	Greedily choose a minimum-\(h\) vertex \(v_1\) in \(B\), remove its red-support nonneighbors \(A_1\), choose a minimum-\(h\) vertex in the remaining common neighborhood, and continue.
136	
137	Since the support on \(B\) is \(K_4\)-free, this process stops after at most three choices. Write
138	\[
139	g_i=W(v_i,\cdot),\qquad x_i=|A_i|,\qquad h_i=h(v_i).
140	\]
141	The sets \(A_i\) partition \(B\), and
142	\[
143	g_i=0\ \hbox{on }A_i,\qquad
144	\sum_i x_i h_i\le s(a-s),\qquad x_i\le b.     \tag{6}
145	\]
146	
147	Essential infima need not be attained. Rigorously, choose \(\varepsilon\)-essential minimizers, avoiding the null exceptional fibers in (1). The middle inequality in (6) then has an added \(+\varepsilon\). All estimates below are continuous in finitely many bounded moments, so passing to a subsequence and then letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) gives the stated inequalities. We henceforth suppress these vanishing errors.
148	
149	There cannot be just one choice, since then \(b\ge|B|=1-s>3/4\).
150	
151	There cannot be just two choices either. If \(s=0\), their summed blue row bounds immediately give \(2b\ge1\). Otherwise put
152	\[
153	H=\int_R(g_1^2+g_2^2),\qquad m=\int_R(g_1+g_2).
154	\]
155	Because \(x_1+x_2=1-s\) and \(x_i\le b\), (6) gives
156	\[
157	H\le\frac{s(a-s)}{1-s-b}.
158	\]
159	Writing
160	\[
161	q^2=\frac{a-s}{2(1-s-b)}\le a=u^2,
162	\]
163	Cauchy–Schwarz and the summed blue bounds yield
164	\[
165	2b\ge1+s-2\sqrt{2sH}+H
166	   \ge1+s(1-4u+2u^2).                       \tag{7}
167	\]
168	If \(u\le1-1/\sqrt2\), this contradicts \(b<1/2\). Otherwise \(s\le a\) implies
169	\[
170	b\ge\frac12+a\left(\frac12+a-2u\right)\ge(1-u)^2,
171	\]
172	because the difference in the last inequality is
173	\[
174	\frac{(u^2-1)(2u^2-4u+1)}2\ge0.
175	\]
176	Again this is a contradiction.
177	
178	Thus three rows are selected. Applying (5) to their triangle shows \(a>1/12\). If \(a\ge1/9\), its optimizing choice \(r=1/\sqrt a-1\le2\) contradicts the hypothesis again. Hence
179	\[
180	\frac1{12}<a<\frac19.                       \tag{8}
181	\]
182	
183	## 4. The adaptive three-row inequality
184	
185	This section supplies the intermediate-range upper bound.
186	
187	Write \(u=\sqrt a\), so \(1/\sqrt{12}<u<1/3\), and set
188	\[
189	\begin{gathered}
190	t=2\sqrt3u,\quad
191	\kappa=3-\frac{2\sqrt3-3}{u},\quad
192	\ell=\frac4t-2,\quad K=3-t,\\
193	c_0=3-\frac{\sqrt3-1}{u},\qquad
194	\ell_i=\frac4{t+\kappa h_i}-2.
195	\end{gathered}
196	\]
197	On this interval,
198	\[
199	\frac43<\kappa<\frac53,\qquad c_0>0,\qquad
200	0\le\ell_i\le2.                             \tag{9}
201	\]
202	For the last assertion, \(h_i\le s\le a\le1/9\), so
203	\[
204	1\le t+\kappa h_i
205	 \le\frac2{\sqrt3}+\frac5{27}<2.
206	\]
207	
208	Let
209	\[
210	M_i=\int_R g_jg_k,\qquad \{i,j,k\}=\{1,2,3\}.
211	\]
212	On \(A_i\), the coordinate \(g_i\) vanishes. The elementary inequality
213	\[
214	1+(1-x)^2+(1-y)^2+\lambda xy
215	 \ge3-\frac4{2+\lambda}\qquad(0\le\lambda\le2)       \tag{10}
216	\]
217	therefore gives, after integrating and using (1) and (6),
218	\[
219	3b\ge
220	(1-s)K-\kappa s(a-s)
221	-a\sum_i\ell_i+\sum_i\ell_iM_i
222	+\int_R\sum_i(1-g_i)^2.                     \tag{11}
223	\]
224	The exact square identity behind (10) is
225	\[
226	\frac{2+\lambda}{4}
227	 \left(x+y-\frac4{2+\lambda}\right)^2
228	+\frac{2-\lambda}{4}(x-y)^2.
229	\]
230	
231	If \(s=0\), (11) immediately gives \(b\ge f(a)\). Assume \(s>0\), and let \(\mathbb E_R\) denote normalized expectation on \(R\). Put
232	\[
233	G=g_1+g_2+g_3,\qquad
234	Q=\mathbb E_R(g_1^2+g_2^2+g_3^2),
235	\]
236	and define the nonnegative quantity
237	\[
238	\mathcal E=
239	\mathbb E_R\left[
240	 \frac{(G-3u)^2}{3u}
241	 +c_0\left(g_1^2+g_2^2+g_3^2-\frac{G^2}{3}\right)
242	\right].                                   \tag{12}
243	\]
244	
245	A rearrangement of (11) gives
246	\[
247	3b-3f(a)\ge
248	s\mathcal E+3su(u_*-u)+\kappa s^2-P,         \tag{13}
249	\]
250	where, with \(H=h_1+h_2+h_3=sQ\),
251	\[
252	P=\sum_i\left[
253	 \frac{\kappa^2h_i^2}{3(t+\kappa h_i)}
254	 +\frac{4\kappa h_iM_i}{t(t+\kappa h_i)}
255	\right].
256	\]
257	We now verify
258	\[
259	s\mathcal E+\kappa s^2-P\ge0.                \tag{14}
260	\]
261	
262	### 4.1. Bounding the error \(P\)
263	
264	Since \(M_i\le(h_j+h_k)/2\), put
265	\[
266	A_0=\frac{\kappa^2}{3t},\qquad B_0=\frac{2\kappa}{t^2}.
267	\]
268	Then
269	\[
270	P\le A_0\sum h_i^2+B_0\left(H^2-\sum h_i^2\right).
271	\]
272	Here \(B_0\ge A_0\), \(A_0\le25/27\), and \(B_0\le10/3\). Thus
273	\[
274	P\le\frac{A_0+2B_0}{3}H^2
275	 \le\frac{205}{81}s^2Q^2.                  \tag{15}
276	\]
277	
278	### 4.2. A useful bound on \(Q\)
279	
280	For \(0\le x_i\le1/2\), \(\sum x_i=1-s\), and \(0\le r_i\le1\),
281	\[
282	\sum_i x_ir_i\ge\left(\frac12-s\right)
283	                  \left(\sum_i r_i-1\right).       \tag{16}
284	\]
285	One quick proof is to minimize the left side over the weight polytope. Its vertices are permutations of \((1/2,1/2-s,0)\), where (16) is immediate.
286	
287	Apply (16) to \(r_i=g_i(r)^2\), integrate over \(R\), and use (6). It follows that
288	\[
289	Q\le1+\frac{a-s}{1/2-s}\le1+2a\le\frac{11}{9}.       \tag{17}
290	\]
291	
292	### 4.3. The remaining scalar estimate
293	
294	Let
295	\[
296	k=\frac1{\sqrt3u}-1>0.
297	\]
298	Expanding (12) and applying Jensen gives
299	\[
300	\mathcal E\ge k(\mathbb E_RG)^2-2\mathbb E_RG+c_0Q+3u
301	             \ge-\frac1k+c_0Q+3u.           \tag{18}
302	\]
303	For \(Q\ge18/25\), this implies
304	\[
305	\mathcal E-\frac Q4\ge J(u),
306	\quad
307	J(u)=3u-\frac1k+\frac{18}{25}\left(c_0-\frac14\right)>0.       \tag{19}
308	\]
309	Indeed,
310	\[
311	J''(u)=
312	-\frac6{(1-\sqrt3u)^3}
313	-\frac{36(\sqrt3-1)}{25u^3}<0,
314	\]
315	and its values at \(u=1/\sqrt{12}\) and \(u=1/3\) are respectively
316	\[
317	\frac{97\sqrt3-167}{50}>0,\qquad
318	\frac{232-133\sqrt3}{50}>0.
319	\]
320	
321	Combining (9) and (15), the left side of (14), divided by \(s\), is at least
322	\[
323	\mathcal E+s\left(\frac43-\frac{205}{81}Q^2\right).
324	\]
325	This is nonnegative if \(Q\le\sqrt{108/205}\). Otherwise
326	\[
327	Q>\sqrt{108/205}>\frac{18}{25},
328	\]
329	so (17)–(19), together with \(s\le1/9\), give the lower bound
330	\[
331	\frac Q4-\frac19\left(\frac{205}{81}Q^2-\frac43\right)>0.
332	\]
333	This last quadratic is concave in \(Q\); at the endpoints of
334	\([18/25,11/9]\) its values are
335	\[
336	\frac{1231}{6750},\qquad \frac{7943}{236196}.
337	\]
338	This proves (14).
339	
340	Consequently (13) becomes
341	\[
342	b\ge f(a)+su(u_*-u).                        \tag{20}
343	\]
344	If \(u\le u_*\), it gives \(b\ge f(a)\). If \(u\ge u_*\), use \(s\le1\) and
345	\[
346	f(a)+u(u_*-u)=(1-u)^2
347	\]
348	to obtain \(b\ge(1-u)^2\), a contradiction. Thus \(u<u_*\), proving the kernel lemma.
349	
350	## 5. The Ramsey upper bound
351	
352	Define
353	\[
354	C_3(\alpha)=
355	\frac{\bigl(\sqrt{3-2\alpha}+2\sqrt\alpha\bigr)^2}{3},
356	\qquad
357	C_R(\alpha)=(1+\sqrt\alpha)^2,
358	\]
359	and let \(C>\max\{2,C_3(\alpha),C_R(\alpha)\}\).
360	
361	If infinitely many colorings on \(\lfloor Cn\rfloor\) vertices avoided the required books, Section 1 would produce a kernel with
362	\[
363	a=\frac{\alpha}{C},\qquad b=\frac1C.
364	\]
365	These parameters meet the kernel lemma’s hypotheses. Its conclusion gives
366	\[
367	1\ge C+2\alpha-4\sqrt{\frac{\alpha C}{3}}.
368	\]
369	Setting \(y=\sqrt C\) and solving this quadratic inequality yields
370	\[
371	C\le
372	\left(\frac{2\sqrt\alpha+\sqrt{3-2\alpha}}{\sqrt3}\right)^2
373	=C_3(\alpha),
374	\]
375	a contradiction. Therefore
376	\[
377	\limsup_{n\to\infty}
378	\frac{r(B_{\lceil\alpha n\rceil},B_n)}n
379	\le\max\{2,C_3(\alpha),C_R(\alpha)\}.          \tag{21}
380	\]
381	
382	## 6. Matching constructions
383	
384	All three terms in (21) are attained asymptotically.
385	
386	* **The term \(2\).** Take two blue cliques of size \(n+1\), with every cross-edge red. There is no red triangle and no blue \(B_n\).
387	
388	* **The random term.** Color each edge red independently with
389	  \[
390	  p=\frac{\sqrt\alpha}{1+\sqrt\alpha}.
391	  \]
392	  Expected red and blue book sizes are \(p^2N+O(1)\) and \((1-p)^2N+O(1)\). For
393	  \(N=(C_R(\alpha)-\varepsilon)n\), both are below the forbidden sizes by a linear margin.
394	
395	* **The three-part construction.** Partition the vertices into three equal parts. Make every within-part edge blue, and color cross-edges independently red with probability
396	  \[
397	  p=\frac{3\sqrt\alpha}
398	          {\sqrt{3-2\alpha}+2\sqrt\alpha}.
399	  \]
400	  A red edge has expected red book size \(p^2N/3+O(1)\). The largest expected blue book size is
401	  \[
402	  \frac{1+2(1-p)^2}{3}N+O(1),
403	  \]
404	  attained by a within-part blue edge. For a cross-part blue edge the expectation is smaller by \(p^2N/3+O(1)\).
405	  The identities
406	  \[
